opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the "pre-training is dead" narrative got a little ahead of itself. What happened is that for a while, a lot of the public excitement shifted to reasoning and reinforcement learning, and rightly so. Those were huge unlocks. But people took that to mean pre-training had hit a wall, and I don't think that's what the evidence actually shows.

The way I see it, pre-training is still where a model gets most of its world knowledge, its intuitions, and its basic sense of how things fit together. Everything you do afterward, whether it's RL or post-training of any kind, builds on that base. If the base model is stronger, the reasoning you get on top of it is stronger too. These approaches multiply each other. They aren't competing.

There's also a lot of room left in how we do pre-training, not just how much compute we throw at it. Data quality, data mixtures, architecture choices, how you handle long context, how efficiently you use the data you have. When people talk about a "data wall," I think they're imagining that the only way forward is to scrape more of the internet. That's not really how we think about it. There's a lot of algorithmic progress that lets you get more out of the same data, and that's been a big focus for us.

And honestly, part of it is just that pre-training is hard to do well at the frontier. It takes a big, well-coordinated research effort, and some of the slowdown people noticed was really about execution and infrastructure, not some fundamental limit. When you get those things right, you still see the gains. So I'd say pre-training isn't dead. It's just less flashy than it used to be, and it's still a core part of what moves the frontier.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the "pre-training is dead" narrative conflates two different things: the end of easy wins and the end of returns. What people are really reacting to is that the obvious levers, scrape more of the web and scale the cluster, have gotten more expensive and the curves look flatter on the benchmarks we've been staring at for years. That's true. But that's not the same as pre-training no longer mattering.

Here's how I'd frame it. Everything that happens after pre-training, whether it's RL, reasoning, tool use, agentic training, is leveraging the base model's representations. The reason reasoning models work at all is that the base model already has latent capabilities that RL can sharpen and elicit. If you take a weak base model and throw the same RL recipe at it, you don't get the same result. So pre-training sets the ceiling, and post-training determines how much of that ceiling you actually reach. Those two things compound. Better pre-training makes every unit of RL compute go further, and better RL raises the bar for what you'd want the base model to know.

The second thing I'd push on is that "we've run out of data" is a statement about one particular data regime. Yes, high-quality natural language text on the open internet is finite. But the frontier of pre-training is increasingly about data quality, data curation, synthetic data that's actually useful rather than just regurgitated, multimodal data, and importantly, the interaction data that comes out of deploying these systems in the world. The algorithmic side hasn't stalled either. Architecture, optimizers, how you schedule and mix data, how you handle long context, all of these are still delivering real gains per flop. We're nowhere near a theoretical efficiency ceiling.

And honestly, I'd point to the empirical record. Every time someone has declared a scaling regime dead, a new generation of models has come along and surprised people. GPT-4.5 was a pre-training bet, and people underestimated how much of its character and world knowledge and taste came purely from the base. Those qualities are very hard to bolt on afterward.

So my view is that pre-training isn't dead, it's just no longer the only story. It's become one of several axes we scale together, and the frontier is about being good at all of them simultaneously. Declaring it dead because the chart got harder to read is, I think, a mistake people will regret.

astra-6.text:
I think “dead” is too strong. There’s a difference between saying pre-training is getting harder to scale and saying it no longer produces useful improvements. You can see diminishing returns and still get a lot of value from the next increment.

Pre-training gives you the foundation that post-training and inference-time compute build on. If you improve that foundation, you can improve what those later stages are able to do. So I don’t see these as competing explanations for where progress comes from.

The question is how you allocate compute across all of those stages. That balance can shift without pre-training becoming irrelevant. I’m excited about the other directions, but I wouldn’t interpret their success as evidence that we’re done with pre-training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “dead” is too strong. There’s a difference between saying pre-training is getting more expensive or that the easy gains are harder to find, and saying it no longer improves models. You can have diminishing returns and still get very meaningful improvements.

I also don’t see pre-training and post-training as competing explanations for progress. Pre-training gives you a foundation, and post-training teaches the model to use that foundation more effectively. If you improve the underlying model, you can raise the ceiling on what you get from reasoning and reinforcement learning.

So I’m excited about post-training, but I wouldn’t conclude from its success that we’ve exhausted pre-training. The recipe can keep changing—the data, the architecture, the objective. Scaling one fixed recipe isn’t the whole research agenda.
